title: Skills are new features: Building Skill-Centric Harness — Yogendra Miraje, FactSet

summary: Yogendra Miraje, Principal AI Engineer at FactSet, presents on building skill-centric agentic products at enterprise scale. After Anthropic open-sourced the Agent Skills specification, his team abandoned proprietary "blueprints" and adopted skills fully. The talk's central thesis: in agent-first products, skills are the new features—prompts define who the agent is, tools define what it connects to, and skills define how tasks get done. Engineers thus shift from shipping features to shipping harnesses, the vehicles for skills. He demonstrates a minimal harness (skill registry, system prompt, file read tool) using progressive disclosure: only name, description, and path go into the system prompt; the agent reads full skill bodies on demand. Skill descriptions serve as routing signals—trigger words (e.g., PDF vs HTML) decide which skill fires. He stresses cutting skills by user intent rather than data model. A critical production lesson: after a model upgrade, the agent silently stopped obeying skills because the new model focused on the beginning of skill content while critical instructions sat at the end. He frames skills as testable contracts versioned to a model—evals are mandatory and must be rerun on every model upgrade. At scale, past ten skills, embeddings and similarity search or a smaller shortlisting model select relevant skills for the system prompt. Past a hundred, governance across five pillars—admission, ownership, boundaries, lifecycle, and coherence—becomes non-negotiable, borrowing from decades of code practices with human-in-the-loop automation.
whyItMatters: The software engineering and AI concepts in this talk are deeply intertwined because skills sit at the intersection of code-as-artifact and model-as-runtime. Progressive disclosure, skill registries, and trigger-word routing are simultaneously an architecture decision (how the harness loads context and dispatches capabilities) and an AI design decision (how the model discovers, selects, and executes capabilities without explicit code dispatch). Semantic versioning and evals become inseparable when skills are model-versioned contracts: a code governance practice (versioning, deprecation) gains new urgency because model upgrades can silently break behavior without any code change. The governance pillars (admission, ownership, boundaries, lifecycle, coherence) apply code-maturity practices to a fundamentally new artifact class whose behavior is not fully deterministic. Understanding both dimensions together is essential—the engineering patterns (registry, lazy loading, access control, PR review) make skills manageable, while the AI properties (routing via descriptions, model-versioned contracts, embedding-based shortlisting, skill drift) define what makes skills different from traditional software modules and why they need specialized testing, versioning, and scaling strategies.
temporalContext: Video published July 29, 2026; research conducted as of August 23, 2026. Anthropic's Agent Skills Specification was open-sourced prior to the talk, with multiple academic papers on agent skills appearing in early-to-mid 2026 (arXiv papers dated February through July 2026). FactSet announced its AI Blueprint in 2023 and AI-powered solutions (including Portfolio Commentary and Transcript Assistant) in 2024; CEO Sanoke Viswanathan succeeded Snow in September 2025. The speaker's title evolved from Lead ML Engineer (per August 2024 FactSet blog post) to Principal AI Engineer (per 2026 personal website). The talk was delivered at an AI Engineer event, reflecting the emerging discourse around skills as a product architecture pattern distinct from coding-agent skills.

concepts.name: Skills as the New Features (Who/What/How Framing)
concepts.explanation: In agent-first products, prompts define who the agent is, tools define what it connects to, and skills define how a task gets done; skills replace traditional UI features as the locus of business logic.
concepts.importance: This is the talk's central paradigm shift—it reframes the entire product architecture around skills and positions engineers as harness builders rather than feature builders.

concepts.name: Agent Skills Specification (SKILL.md)
concepts.explanation: Anthropic's open standard defining a skill as a directory with a required SKILL.md file containing frontmatter (name, description) for discovery and a Markdown body for instructions, plus optional scripts, references, and assets subdirectories.
concepts.importance: This specification is the technical foundation the speaker's team adopted after abandoning proprietary blueprints; its structure defines the routing metadata, progressive disclosure levels, and capability contract format demonstrated throughout the talk.

concepts.name: Progressive Disclosure for Context Window Management
concepts.explanation: Only skill name, description, and path are loaded into the system prompt at startup (~100 tokens each); the agent reads the full skill body on demand only when the skill is activated.
concepts.importance: Progressive disclosure is the key mechanism that makes skill-centric agents feasible—it prevents context window exhaustion while allowing hundreds of skills to be discoverable, directly mirroring the official specification's architecture.

concepts.name: Trigger Word Routing for Skill Selection
concepts.explanation: Specific words in skill descriptions (e.g., PDF vs HTML in a report skill) cause the agent to select one skill over another; descriptions function as routing signals that the LLM uses to decide skill activation without explicit code dispatch.
concepts.importance: Trigger words are the practical mechanism that makes description-based routing work—without careful trigger word design, the agent may activate the wrong skill or miss activation entirely.

concepts.name: Skills as Model-Versioned Contracts
concepts.explanation: Skills are contracts tied to specific model versions, not static documentation; a model upgrade can silently break skill obedience even when no skill content changed, because different models attend to different parts of the context differently.
concepts.importance: This concept fundamentally distinguishes AI skills from traditional code modules—they are coupled to the model's behavior, making model upgrades a risk event that requires re-validation of the entire skill library.

concepts.name: Skill Evals (Testing as Contracts)
concepts.explanation: Skills without evals are 'wishful thinking'; every skill must have an evaluation suite that is rerun on every model upgrade to detect behavioral drift.
concepts.importance: Evals are the quality gate that makes skills safe to ship—without them, model upgrades silently break production behavior, as demonstrated by the speaker's real production incident.

concepts.name: Model-Upgrade Skill Drift
concepts.explanation: A production failure mode where upgrading the underlying model caused the agent to stop obeying skills: the new model focused on the beginning of skill content while critical instructions sat at the end, leading to silent behavioral regression despite unchanged skill content.
concepts.importance: This is the concrete production war story that motivates treating skills as model-versioned contracts and making evals mandatory—it demonstrates that model behavior is non-deterministic across versions in ways that break prompt-based instructions.

concepts.name: Embeddings-Based Skill Shortlisting
concepts.explanation: Past approximately ten skills, concatenating all skill metadata into the system prompt becomes infeasible; embeddings and similarity search or a smaller shortlisting model are needed to select the most relevant skills to include.
concepts.importance: This is the scaling inflection point where the skill registry transitions from simple concatenation to a search-based retrieval system, introducing a new layer of AI infrastructure (embedding models, vector similarity) into the harness.

concepts.name: Agentic Harnesses vs Coding Agents
concepts.explanation: The talk deliberately distinguishes building skill-centric harnesses for agentic products at enterprise scale from the dominant discourse around coding-agent skills (e.g., Claude Code, CodeEx), filling a gap in product-focused skill architecture.
concepts.importance: This distinction scopes the talk's applicability: the governance and scaling lessons apply to product skills served to end users, not to developer-facing coding skills, which have different consumption patterns and scale constraints.

concepts.name: Engineer Role Shift: Shipping Harnesses not Features
concepts.explanation: In agent-first products, engineers shift from shipping features (screens, buttons, dashboards) to shipping harnesses—smooth vehicles for skills to run—repositioning the engineer's deliverable from user-facing UI to agent-facing infrastructure.
concepts.importance: This role shift reframes the engineer's core competency from UI construction to harness architecture, with direct implications for team structure, skill sets, and product development workflows.

concepts.name: Skill Library Governance at Enterprise Scale
concepts.explanation: At enterprise scale with 100+ skills, governance—spanning admission, ownership, boundaries, lifecycle, and coherence—becomes non-negotiable, borrowing from decades of code-maturity practices with human-in-the-loop automation rather than red tape.
concepts.importance: This concept elevates skill management from an engineering practice to an organizational capability; without governance, skill libraries at enterprise scale become unsearchable, stale, and dangerous.

concepts.name: Skill Registry
concepts.explanation: A catalog of skills with name, description, and path that the agent discovers at runtime; the foundational data structure of a minimal harness enabling progressive disclosure.
concepts.importance: The skill registry is the minimal harness's core component—it is the single source of truth for discoverable capabilities and scales from a simple concatenation to an embeddings-indexed search index as the library grows.

concepts.name: Agentic Loop with Tool Calls
concepts.explanation: The control loop where the model is called with messages and agent tools each turn, appending tool call results until no tool call produces the final output.
concepts.importance: This is the runtime execution model for skill-centric agents; understanding the loop is prerequisite to implementing progressive disclosure and trigger-word routing.

concepts.name: Minimal Harness Architecture
concepts.explanation: A minimal agentic harness requires only three components: a skill registry, a system prompt, and a file read tool (plus bash or sandbox for executable scripts).
concepts.importance: Establishes the minimum viable architecture that engineering teams need to build before adding skill discovery, ensuring teams can start small before investing in search infrastructure.

concepts.name: Semantic Versioning of Skills
concepts.explanation: Skills should follow semantic versioning with deprecation warnings and change logs, treating each version as a release tied to a specific model.
concepts.importance: Versioning is a cornerstone of the lifecycle governance pillar, enabling teams to track behavioral changes across model upgrades and roll back safely.

concepts.name: PR Review Analog for Skill Admission
concepts.explanation: New skills must pass an admission process using automated git workflows with human-in-the-loop review, directly analogous to pull request review in traditional codebases.
concepts.importance: Admission governance prevents skill sprawl and ensures quality at the point of creation, mirroring proven code-review practices that prevent bad code from entering production.

concepts.name: Named Skill Owners (Code Owners Analog)
concepts.explanation: Every skill must have named maintainers accountable for its content and behavior, analogous to code owners in repository governance systems.
concepts.importance: Without explicit ownership, skills become orphaned and stale; named maintainers ensure accountability and a known escalation path when skills drift or break.

concepts.name: Allow-listed Tools and Access Control (Boundaries)
concepts.explanation: Skills are constrained by allow-listed tools and access control policies, defining what data and capabilities each skill may touch.
concepts.importance: Boundaries governance prevents unauthorized tool usage and data access, forming the security perimeter around individual skills in a shared library.

concepts.name: Periodic Audits for Skill Coherence
concepts.explanation: Skills require periodic audits and automated validation checks to ensure the library remains coherent, with no duplicate or contradictory skills.
concepts.importance: Coherence governance prevents the skill library from degrading into an unsearchable, conflicting mess as it grows past a hundred skills at enterprise scale.

concepts.name: Skill Governance Pillars
concepts.explanation: Five governance dimensions for skill library management at scale: admission (should the skill exist), ownership (named maintainers), boundaries (access control), lifecycle (versioning and deprecation), and coherence (periodic audits).
concepts.importance: This framework structures enterprise-scale skill management, borrowing decades-old code governance practices and adapting them to the unique properties of AI skills as model-versioned contracts.

concepts.name: Slicing by User Intent vs Data Model
concepts.explanation: Skills should be decomposed by user intent (e.g., earnings preparation, pre-market briefing) rather than by data model (e.g., estimate analysis, analyst ratings), refactoring as real use cases emerge.
concepts.importance: This API design principle ensures skills align to how users actually interact with the agent, improving routing accuracy and reducing description ambiguity that causes wrong skill activation.

sections.title: From blueprints to skills
sections.summary: Yogi introduces himself as Principal AI Engineer at FactSet. His prior year's talk covered blueprints—simple step recipes handed to agents—which were essentially naive skills. After Anthropic open-sourced skills, his team adopted them fully instead of maintaining their own standard.

sections.title: Building skill centric agents
sections.summary: He distinguishes his focus from online discourse about coding-agent skills (Claude Code, CodeEx), targeting instead skills in agentic products built on custom harnesses at enterprise scale. Most discourse covers coding agents; he fills the gap for product skills.

sections.title: Skills in context at enterprise scale
sections.summary: Traditional products were surfaces of screens, buttons, and dashboards navigated by users. Now agents are at the forefront, either talking to users or making decisions behind the scenes.

sections.title: Skills as the new features
sections.summary: The who/what/how framing: prompts define who the agent is, tools define what it connects to, skills define how a task gets done. Skills hold business logic and are the new features. Engineers shift from shipping features to shipping harnesses. Equity research and wealth management, formerly buttons and screens, are now skills.

sections.title: Inside a skill: the skill.md
sections.summary: skill.md is the heart. Name and description in front matter enable discovery; body contains business logic, instructions, and references to files and scripts. Simple skills are just markdown; complex ones include executable scripts.

sections.title: A minimal skill registry
sections.summary: Bare minimum harness support requires a skill registry, system prompt, and file read tool (plus bash or sandbox for scripts). Registry is a collection of skills with name, description, and path. Demo uses company research, report HTML, and report PDF skills.

sections.title: Progressive disclosure
sections.summary: Agent discovers skills by concatenating name, description, and path into the system prompt, not the full body. The agentic loop runs with messages and tools, appending tool calls until output. Agent picks relevant skills and reads only those bodies. Example: asking for an NVDA report triggers company_research then report HTML.

sections.title: Trigger words and routing
sections.summary: Descriptions are routing signals. The report PDF skill fires only when the user says PDF—that trigger word routes the agent. Keep descriptions aligned to user requests (not about the skill itself), keep them distinct, and don't let skills go stale. Most product skills are model-driven only, avoiding cognitive load for non-technical users. Cut by user intent, not data model (e.g., earnings preparation instead of estimate analysis; pre-market briefing instead of separate news and analyst rating skills).

sections.title: Skills without evals drift
sections.summary: A model upgrade caused agent failures despite unchanged skill content—the new model focused on the beginning while critical instructions were at the end. Skills without evals are wishful thinking. Skills are contracts versioned to a model, not documentation; rerun evals on every model upgrade.

sections.title: Search and embeddings past ten skills
sections.summary: Shoving all skills in the system prompt works for a few skills but falls apart past roughly ten. Solutions include embeddings with similarity search or a smaller model to shortlist relevant skills for the system prompt.

sections.title: Governance past a hundred skills
sections.summary: Past a hundred skills, hierarchy, metadata filters, and governance are needed. Five governance aspects: admission (should the skill exist, automated git with human in the loop analogous to PR review), ownership (named skill maintainers like code owners), lifecycle (semantic versioning, deprecation warnings, change logs), boundaries (allow-listed tools, access control), and coherence (periodic audits, validation checks). Governance need not be red tape when automated with human-in-the-loop, borrowing from decades of code practices.

sections.title: Skills as the product interface
sections.summary: Takeaways: skills are features in agentic products; engineers ship harnesses not features; routing mechanism doesn't just tune at scale, it changes the mechanism itself; governance is non-negotiable at enterprise scale.

organization.name: FactSet
organization.summary: FactSet is a publicly traded financial data and analytics company (NYSE: FDS, S&P 500 member since December 2021) headquartered in Norwalk, Connecticut, founded in 1978 with approximately 9,263 employees. The speaker, Yogendra Miraje (Principal AI Engineer, GenAI team), builds skill-centric agentic products at FactSet. FactSet launched 'FactSet Intelligence,' a multi-layered AI stack combining data, agents, and reimagined workflows with MCP-enabled data infrastructure, orchestration, evaluation, and quality controls. Products include FactSet Mercury (conversational LLM agent for banker workflows), AI for Banking, and AI for Wealth. The talk's enterprise-scale skill governance practices, financial use cases (equity research, wealth management, earnings preparation), and agent harness architecture all originate from FactSet's production environment. CEO transition occurred in September 2025 when Snow retired and was succeeded by Sanoke Viswanathan.

technologies.label: Agent Skills Specification (SKILL.md)
technologies.summary: Anthropic's open-sourced specification defining modular agent capabilities as directories containing a required SKILL.md file. The frontmatter (name, description) serves as routing signals for skill discovery; the Markdown body contains business logic and instructions; optional scripts, references, and assets subdirectories extend capabilities. The speaker's FactSet team adopted this specification after abandoning proprietary 'blueprints,' since maintaining their own standard was redundant once Anthropic's open standard existed. The specification defines the file format, progressive disclosure architecture, routing via descriptions, and capability contract format that all subsequent patterns in the talk build upon.
technologies.role: The adopted open standard that replaced proprietary blueprints; the technical foundation for the talk's skill registry, progressive disclosure, and routing demonstrations. The speaker explicitly frames his team's adoption of this specification as the pivotal decision that shaped their entire product architecture.

technologies.label: Skill-Centric Agent Harness Architecture
technologies.summary: A minimal architecture for agent-first products comprising three components: a skill registry, a system prompt, and a file read tool (plus bash or sandbox for executable scripts). The harness uses progressive disclosure—injecting only skill name, description, and path into the system prompt—and an agentic loop that calls the model with messages and tools each turn until no more tool calls are produced. Trigger words in skill descriptions serve as routing signals selecting which skill activates. The speaker positions this architecture as the shift from shipping features to shipping harnesses, where engineers build the smooth vehicles for skills to run rather than user-facing UI.
technologies.role: The central technical demonstration of the talk: a minimal harness with a skill registry (company_research, report HTML, report PDF skills), system prompt with progressive disclosure, and agentic loop that picks relevant skills and reads their bodies on demand

technologies.label: Embeddings-Based Skill Shortlisting
technologies.summary: A retrieval technique for scaling skill-centric agents past approximately ten skills, at which point concatenating all skill metadata into the system prompt becomes infeasible. The approach uses embeddings and similarity search, or alternatively a smaller shortlisting model, to select the most relevant skills per user request and include only those in the system prompt. This introduces a retrieval layer between the user's request and the skill registry, changing the routing mechanism from direct concatenation to semantic search. The technique is presented as a scaling inflection point where skill discovery transitions from a prompt-engineering problem to an information-retrieval problem.
technologies.role: The recommended scaling mechanism past ten skills; the inflection point where direct skill concatenation in the system prompt fails and semantic search infrastructure becomes necessary

technologies.label: Skill Library Governance Framework
technologies.summary: An organizational architecture for managing skill libraries at enterprise scale (past one hundred skills), comprising five governance pillars: admission (should the skill exist, via automated git with human-in-the-loop analogous to PR review), ownership (named skill maintainers like code owners), boundaries (allow-listed tools and access control), lifecycle (semantic versioning, deprecation warnings, change logs), and coherence (periodic audits and validation checks). The framework borrows decades-old code-maturity practices and adapts them to the unique properties of AI skills as model-versioned contracts whose behavior is non-deterministic across model versions. Governance is framed as non-red-tape when properly automated with human-in-the-loop processes.
technologies.role: The enterprise-scale management framework presented as the final and most critical lesson: past one hundred skills, governance across five pillars becomes non-negotiable. The speaker frames this as borrowing from decades of code-maturity practices adapted to model-versioned skill contracts.

evidence.excerpt: we are only using the name and description path in this system prompt and not the skill body and that's what what they call about is progressive disclosure
evidence.supports: Progressive disclosure means the system prompt contains only skill metadata, not full skill bodies

evidence.excerpt: descriptions are really the routing signals
evidence.supports: Skill descriptions function as routing signals that determine which skill the agent activates

evidence.excerpt: skills without evals are really just wishful thinking
evidence.supports: Skills require evals to prevent drift when models are upgraded

evidence.excerpt: skills are really the contracts versioned to a model
evidence.supports: Skills are contracts tied to specific model versions, not documentation

evidence.excerpt: When you have like more than 10 skill, maybe that's like a good point to think start thinking about... having embeddings and have similarity search and short lists
evidence.supports: Past ten skills, embeddings and similarity search or a smaller shortlisting model are needed to select skills for the system prompt

evidence.excerpt: there are like five aspect of skill library governance and these are admission, ownership, boundaries, life cycle and coherence
evidence.supports: Five governance pillars are needed for skill library management at scale

evidence.excerpt: at enterprise scale the skill library governance is really non-negotiable
evidence.supports: Governance is mandatory at enterprise scale regardless of implementation approach
